Raspberry Pi 4 · Arduino · nRF24L01 · a door, a desk and a calendar

A light on the office door that reads the room

An inverted‑U of six NeoPixels sits above the office door showing one of four states — off, green, yellow, red. Inside the office, a 3.4‑inch round touchscreen on a Pi 4 sets that state by hand, and sets it on its own from a private calendar feed: ten minutes before a meeting you accepted the whole face washes amber, two minutes before it goes crimson and the door turns red.

All three pieces are built and talking over the air: the light on the door, a handheld remote, and the dashboard with its own radio hat. The panel below is that dashboard as it runs today, wired to a simulation of the light and the remote across the same four‑byte radio protocol the hardware speaks. Everything on it responds — even pulling the light's plug.

What it does

The door

Four states and an easter egg

Off, green, yellow, red, plus a party mode the firmware enters on five OFF presses — from either the remote or the panel. The two bottom pixels are mirrored and carry the power state instead of the selection, so charging and a low battery read from across the room.

The pages

A swipe away: the day, the forecast, the system's health

The face is the middle of a row of pages. Tap the time, or swipe left, for the rest of today: the hours down the page, meetings as blocks to scale, the gaps called out - FREE UNTIL 1:30 PM. One page further, or a tap on the weather line, and the next 24 hours, 10 days or the air quality arrive behind three tabs, as bars that scroll - temperature above the line, rain and wind below, sunrise and sunset where they fall. A storm warning takes the weather line's place and a banner under the date; smoke puts the AQI on the line from 101. One page further is health: the Pi's temperature and wifi as gauges, then the light, the remote, the calendar, the network, the weather and the printer. When something there wants a look a dot glows at ten o'clock and slides straight to it. The arc and the dial never move; a tap on the small clock or five minutes untouched brings the face back. A meeting alert does too, when it starts and when it turns red, then lets go - and for the last 30 seconds before the meeting the face is locked.

Debug pages

Everything it can fake, one swipe the other way

Swipe right from the face for three pages of fakes: the meeting alert, the day - empty, one made-up meeting, or a whole busy one for the agenda -, the network, health and the dismiss prompt; the forecast, a weather alert, smoke and the printer's states; the light's battery and its radio - weak, or not answering at all; and the background. Each press sets one and slides to where it shows, and CLEAR ALL puts everything back. While anything is faked a DEBUG pill sits under the card. A faked red alert is the face only - it never reaches the door. They replaced every keyboard shortcut, because the panel has no keyboard.

The printer

A camera window, and a printer that can ask for you

While the Prusa Core One+ prints, a button at two o'clock carries its progress as a ring and says what is next - COLOR 38M, HEATING. Tap it and the camera opens in a window, at the camera's own 24 fps on the panel, with chips over the empty bed for nozzle and bed, when it will be done, the model and the next color change. When PrusaLink reports ATTENTION or ERROR a crimson glow breathes behind the button or round the window, and a color change says so: COLOR CHANGE · LOAD THE NEXT FILAMENT. When the print finishes the button turns green and breathes until it is tapped or the next print starts. ffmpeg runs only while the window is open.

The dial

Controls that follow the arc

Four detents on the lower 168° of the rim. A straight four‑across row gets only 394 px of chord on a round panel and caps each tab near 90 px; following the arc gives each control ~270 px. The tapped detent expands out of its own tick while the one you left collapses back into its, both on the same 0.28 s clock.

The calendar

Only a meeting you accepted turns the light red

The parser resolves your own attendance and never borrows another attendee's. Red needs an explicit PARTSTAT=ACCEPTED or you as organiser, and a timed event. Everything else still shows on the card and still gets the amber heads‑up — only the physical light is held back.

The calendar

Lunch does not exist

Titles on the ignore list, lunch by default, are dropped as the feed is read, the same way declined and cancelled meetings are. They never hold the card, never count toward the day and never raise the light. Before, lunch stayed on the card with its alerts muted, and held it for ten minutes while the next meeting waited.

The card

One meeting fades into the next

When the card changes subject, the countdown and title fade out over 0.4 s, swap, and fade back in. Only the text waits: the arc and the alerts still follow the calendar, so a fade can never delay a warning. The empty day is a subject too.

The card

The meeting that matters, not the earliest

Of the occurrences that have not ended, the card takes the first that began less than ten minutes ago — so anything still to come wins at once, and a meeting under way keeps the card only for its first ten minutes. It fixed a real hole: a 10:30 standup inside a 9–11 block used to get no warning at all.

The card

Unconfirmed meetings say so

A tentative invitation — or one you have not answered — is prefixed TENTATIVE · and never raises the light. A tap on the card offers to drop that occurrence: nothing is declined and no reply is sent, the instance is simply filtered out from then on. Accepted meetings are never offered.

The countdown

A ring that moves every frame

The T- readout and the perimeter arc both count down from the occurrence's absolute start rather than from a polled snapshot, so their resolution is the frame rate. One second of arc is 0.6° — 47 pixels — so only that band is repainted, never the 21,000 px ring.

The face

Weather, and a scrim that earns its keep

Temperature and condition come from open‑meteo every fifteen minutes. The dark wash across the middle is load‑bearing rather than decorative: the clock is 200‑weight at 208 px and a 2 px line drawn through those numerals destroys them.

The card

A tap only asks

The confirmation opens in two movements: a bright point grows into a vertical line the panel's height, then the panel unfolds sideways out of that line while the seam fades. It is modal — its buttons sit directly over the dial's annulus, so it has to answer before the dial does, and a tap while it is still growing is swallowed rather than guessed at.

The dial

Party mode has no detent

Party is command 4 and the dial has four slots, so nothing is selected — the selection chases instead, each detent rising and falling in its own hue. It starts on OFF, because that is where the dial already was, and the total lit ink is constant so the ring travels without pulsing.

The network

Offline says so, and a tap fixes it

After two failed probes 30 s apart, a pill appears above the clock. Tapping it runs four steps: check again, rejoin wifi through NetworkManager, wait for a route, and refetch both feeds. Each step shows on the pill with a segment bar, and it ends BACK ONLINE or with the reason it failed.

The panel

A hidden way to shut down

Hold the clock for three seconds. A thin ring sweeps just inside the rim, and lifting or sliding off early cancels. Even then it only asks. A confirmed shutdown runs systemctl poweroff, so the SD card is never pulled mid‑write.

The panel

Composed on the graphics chip

The CPU draws only the background art; every other layer — the scrim, the dial, the type, the alert wash, the sheen — is a texture the Pi's GPU blends, read back to within a few counts of the software version. A frame went from 16–36 ms to 7–24, so the panel holds 30 FPS even when idle, synced to the panel's 63 Hz so nothing tears, on 41% of a core.

The radio

A tap never flickers back

The light used to queue up its replies, so the first poll after a tap reported the state from before it and the dial bounced back for half a second. The firmware now keeps exactly one reply staged, and for three seconds after a command the dashboard treats a reply showing the old state as stale — while still believing anything else, like party mode, at once.

The radio

Pull the light's plug and the panel knows

Three unanswered polls — about three seconds — and the dial shows OFF, which is also what the light boots into, so nothing needs correcting when it comes back. While it is gone the radio gives up after two quick retries instead of fifteen, so the panel does not stutter once a second. Try Unplug light in the power controls.

The panel

No desktop, no window manager

The Pi boots to a multi‑user target and starts the app directly on the display, which halved idle CPU from 49% of a core to 24%. Power‑on to a usable face is 26 seconds, most of it systemd rather than the app.

Honesty

A dead feed is not an empty day

Both pollers record their last success. After five missed calendar polls or a forty‑minute weather gap, the town's name on the weather line gives way to an amber notice — CAL 25 MIN OLD, WX 45 MIN OLD — and an empty day with the calendar down says Calendar not updating rather than “Schedule clear”, which would be a lie. The face's debug page has a STALE row to show it.

Eight backgrounds, one an hour

Behind the clock, eight styles take turns an hour each, and a tap on the date skips to the next. Each is reseeded on every turn, so none repeats a composition. No two of the sky‑themed ones run back to back, the two grid‑and‑cells faces are never beside each other, and a change waits while an alert is running. A handover fades the old one out, holds a beat, and fades the new one in — never both at half, since the styles are nowhere near equal in brightness. Every one was judged on the panel by eye, and the ones ported from a design page are checked against it frame by frame.

1 · Sky · Arc

A window onto a turning sky

Six thousand stars on a disc whose axis is 1,500 px away, drifting at 5 px a second, with 45 constellations built as small graphs — they fork and close, and no two lines ever cross. Stars are drawn at sub‑pixel positions, so the field never jiggles as it moves.

2 · Snake · Bars

Three snakes that play for real

Each takes the shortest path to its own glowing pellet around every body on a round board of 437 cells, treats the others' pellets as walls, and grows a step after it eats. Out of room or at full length it fades out and a new game fades in. The pellet keeps its glow until the bar has covered it.

3 · Moon · Crescent

The real near side, through its phases

NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter maps — its camera mosaic for the seas and highlands, its laser altimeter for the craters along the shadow line — through a full cycle every ten minutes, shaded the way regolith actually scatters, so the full moon is flat rather than a lit ball. Mare Imbrium sits behind the numerals.

4 · Life · Trails

Conway's Life, with a long exposure

A 64² torus, one generation every 1.2 s, each cell a dot that leaves a fading trail. A birth arrives at once and a death fades, and every three minutes a disc of fresh soup keeps the field from settling. Generations come off an integer count, so a dropped frame never changes the future.

5 · Topo · Survey

A contour sheet on the move

Hills larger than the panel drifting at 4 px a second while the terrain reshapes over a quarter of an hour, every fifth contour heavier and labelled with its elevation, summits marked with spot heights. Labels follow their own contour and fade in and out over 1.5 s rather than popping.

6 · Dawn · Line

Sunrise on the lunar surface

Sixty ridgelines from the horizon to your feet, each drawn only where it rises above the nearer ones, the way a plotter draws terrain. The light sweeps toward you, holds, and the shadow follows from the horizon; the stars come out one at a time as the plain goes dark, brightest first.

7 · Board · Dense

A circuit board with traffic

Traces on a 46 px grid, footprints, pours and via stitching, with seven glowing signals travelling its runs at a time and single pads blinking between them. A fresh board every two minutes.

8 · Defrag · Clusters

The Windows 95 cluster map

520 clusters being defragmented — read, carried and written one at a time — then used for a while, files deleted and written into the gaps, and defragmented again, forever. The disk stays between a third and two thirds full, and the cells behind the weather and the meeting card quieten so the type stays crisp.

How the three pieces talk

An nRF24L01's only return channel is the ack payload it sends back automatically, and the hardware acks from the payload staged before your packet arrived. So a command's ack can never confirm that command: the dashboard sets the state optimistically, throws the ack away, and believes the next query instead.

0xFF is a query, deliberately not a command — the firmware recognises it and does nothing. Polling used to re‑assert the current state, which while the light was off meant a command‑0 packet, counted as an OFF press, and five polls drove the light into party mode by itself.

Party mode is the receiver's rule, not the dashboard's. The firmware counts the presses; the panel finds out from the next poll, within a second, because nothing pushes.

The light reads one packet per pass of its loop, and its radio holds up to three staged replies and sends the oldest — so once packets had arrived faster than it read them, every reply ran several packets behind, for good. On the hat's first day a tap bounced the dial back for half a second. The firmware now flushes before it stages, keeping exactly one reply, and the dashboard gives a command three seconds' grace against a reply that still shows the state from before it.

The command byte, shared by all four files
ValueCommandLightRemotePanel
0Offyes — 5× → partyyesyes
1Greenyesyesyes
2Yellowyesyesyes
3Redyesyesyes — and automatic
4Partyyesn/an/a
0xFFQueryreports, changes nothingn/aevery second

The hardware

PieceBoardWhat it isState
The lightArduino Nano Six NeoPixels in an inverted U, nRF24 listener, battery and USB sensing Built and deployed above the door
The remotePro Mini 3.3V/8MHz Four buttons, deep sleep, pin‑change wake, on a CR2032 with 100 µF across its radio Built and working over the air
The dashboardPi 4B Waveshare 3.4″ 800×800 round touchscreen, boots headless straight into the app in 26 s On the desk
The radio hatCustom PCB nRF24 module on SPI, fed by its own AP2112 3.3 V regulator from the Pi's 5 V Built and driving the light

The panel is 800×800 spanning a 3.4‑inch circle, so the whole design is measured in panel pixels and confirmed by eye on the hardware rather than in a browser. Composed on the GPU, a frame costs 7–24 ms depending on the background; the panel holds 30 FPS at idle and through an alert on about 41% of one core, and could run at 73–84 FPS uncapped. An alert wash, once the most expensive frame in the project, now costs nothing measurable.
